title: Abolitionism and Women's Rights
summary: What made 1830s abolitionism new (immediate emancipation), its strategies and leaders (Walker, Garrison, Maria Stewart, the Grimké sisters, Douglass, Sojourner Truth), how women's antislavery work turned into a women's rights movement, and the Seneca Falls Declaration of Sentiments. Includes both class discussions (Angelina Grimké; Seneca Falls).
sourceNote: Dr. Jeffrey's lectures 'Cherokee & Abolitionism' (abolition slides) and 'Abolitionism & Women's Rights' (Sep 21 and 23), with the class discussions on Angelina Grimké's 'Human Rights not founded on Sex' and the Seneca Falls Declaration of Sentiments. Dates not on the slides are the standard ones.

sections.heading: The big picture: one movement grows out of another

blocks.md: **Abolitionism** is the movement to end slavery. The lecture defines the new abolitionism of the **1830s** by one word: **immediate**. Earlier reformers wanted slavery to end slowly, or wanted freed Black people sent to Africa. The 1830s abolitionists demanded **immediate emancipation**, now, with no payment to slaveholders.

**Women's rights** grew straight out of that work. Women ran petition drives and gave speeches against slavery, were told to be quiet because they were women, and started asking about their own rights. The lecture's line: the women's rights movement came out of antislavery activism.

data.question: How did a fight against **slavery** become a fight for **women's rights** too?

blocks.md: **Why it matters.** This is where American reform learns its methods: petitions, newspapers, speaking tours, conventions, and quoting the Declaration of Independence back at the country. Every later rights movement, including ones today, uses the same toolkit.
blocks.label: why

blocks.body: The 1830s demand that slavery end **at once**, not gradually, and without paying slaveholders. **Example:** Garrison's Liberator: 'I will not retreat a single inch, and I will be heard.'

The older approach: end slavery slowly (often child by child, as northern states did), or 'colonize' freed Black Americans in Africa (the American Colonization Society, 1816). 1830s abolitionists, Black and white, **rejected** both.

sections.heading: Angelina Grimké: 'Human Rights not founded on Sex'

blocks.md: Angelina Grimké grew up in a slaveholding family in Charleston, saw slavery up close, moved north, and became a Quaker and an abolitionist. When she and her sister Sarah lectured to mixed audiences in 1837, ministers and writers attacked them for stepping outside 'woman's sphere'. The class-discussion reading is her reply (1837, to the educator Catharine Beecher).

blocks.body: Rights come from being a **moral human being**, not from being male or female, so whatever is morally right for a man to do is morally right for a woman to do, including speaking against slavery.

blocks.md: **Key phrases to quote** (the discussion asks for them): 'Human beings have rights, because they are moral beings'; 'whatever it is morally right for man to do, it is morally right for woman to do'; and her refusal to recognize separate 'men's rights and women's rights', only **human rights**.

**See the connection.** Her argument against sexism is the **same** argument as her argument against slavery: rights belong to every moral being. That's why defending her right to speak about slavery turned into a defense of women's rights. The two movements share one logic.
blocks.label: think

blocks.md: **Historical context (Q2).** 1837: immediate abolition was only six years old and often met with mobs. The 'separate spheres' ideal (see the Market Revolution chapter) said respectable women belonged at home. Women were already doing much of the petition work. So a southern-born woman lecturing northern men about slavery broke two rules at once, and her critics went after the second one.

blocks.prompt: What is Angelina Grimké's central argument in 'Human Rights not founded on Sex'?
blocks.answer: Rights come from being a **moral being**, not from sex, so what is morally right for a man to do is morally right for a woman to do: there are only **human rights**.

blocks.prompt: Why were the Grimké sisters unusual among abolitionists?
blocks.answer: They were white women from a **southern slaveholding family** (South Carolina), the only ones in the movement, and they spoke to mixed audiences.

blocks.body: The legal rule that a married woman's identity was absorbed into her husband's. The lecture's list: women could **not own property** once married, could not **testify** in court, and could not **make contracts**; a married woman was treated almost as her husband's property. **Example:** a wife's wages legally belonged to her husband.

blocks.md: **The 1840 split.** Abolitionists argued over whether women should hold leadership roles. When women were given a place in the American Anti-Slavery Society, those who objected walked out and formed the **American and Foreign Anti-Slavery Society** (1840). That same year, at the **World Anti-Slavery Convention in London**, women delegates, including **Lucretia Mott**, were refused seats. **Elizabeth Cady Stanton**, there with her husband, met Mott, and they resolved to hold a convention on women's rights.

blocks.answer: The legal rule that absorbed a married woman into her husband: she couldn't own property, testify, or make contracts.

blocks.prompt: What happened in 1840, and why does it matter for women's rights?
blocks.answer: The abolition movement **split** over women's role, and women were **barred** at the London convention, where Mott and Stanton met and decided to organize for women's rights.

sections.heading: Seneca Falls and the Declaration of Sentiments (1848)

blocks.md: On **July 19 and 20, 1848**, about 300 people met at **Seneca Falls, New York**. The convention adopted the **Declaration of Sentiments**, written mainly by Stanton, and about 100 people (68 women and 32 men) signed it.

rows.label: Who is the tyrant
rows.right: '**man**', who has held 'absolute tyranny' over woman

rows.label: The evidence
rows.right: Grievances against men: no vote, no property once married, no divorce or custody rights, shut out of colleges and most jobs

blocks.caption: How the delegates used language (Discussion Q1): they copied the country's most respected document, so rejecting their demands meant rejecting 1776. The form **is** the critique of American democracy.

blocks.md: **The concerns for women's equality (Discussion Q2).** The grievances cover: the **vote** (women had to obey laws they had no voice in making); **property and wages** (taken by the husband); **marriage and divorce** law and **child custody** (favoring men); **education** (colleges closed to women); **jobs** (most professions closed); the **church** (shut out of the ministry); and the **double standard** in morals. The one resolution that almost failed was the demand for the **vote**; it passed after **Frederick Douglass** spoke for it.

blocks.body: Seneca Falls did not win women the vote. It **demanded** it. Nationally, women won the vote only with the 19th Amendment in 1920. In the short run the gains were state laws, like New York's in 1860.

blocks.md: **Results before the Civil War.** In 1854 Stanton addressed the **New York legislature**; in **1860** New York expanded married women's property rights, giving them rights to their own **wages** and joint **custody** of their children. Then, the lecture notes, women **set aside** their own campaign during the Civil War to support the Union and emancipation.

**Where you see it today.** Rewriting a famous text to expose who it leaves out is still a standard protest technique, and the Seneca Falls list of grievances reads like the agenda of the next 170 years: voting, pay, property, custody, education, jobs.
blocks.label: world

blocks.prompt: How did the Seneca Falls delegates use the Declaration of Independence?
blocks.answer: They **copied its structure and language**, adding 'and women' and listing grievances against men instead of the King, so their demands rested on the nation's founding principle.

blocks.prompt: Which Seneca Falls resolution was the most controversial, and who helped it pass?
blocks.answer: The demand for **the vote**; **Frederick Douglass** spoke for it.

blocks.prompt: Who was the first woman to address a mixed audience of men and women (1832)?
What organization did the anti-women faction form in 1840?
What did New York's 1860 law give married women?
blocks.answer: Rights to their own **wages** and joint **custody** of their children, expanding their property rights.

blocks.prompt: When did Susan B. Anthony meet Elizabeth Cady Stanton?
What did women do with their own campaign during the Civil War?
blocks.answer: They **set it aside** to support the war effort and emancipation.

exercises.title: Discussion: Grimké's argument and key phrases
exercises.prompt: In 4 to 5 sentences, state Angelina Grimké's argument in 'Human Rights not founded on Sex' and quote or closely paraphrase two key phrases.
hints: An argument is a claim plus a reason. Her claim is about who has rights; her reason is about what makes someone a rights-holder.
Weak answers say 'she argues for women's rights'. Stronger: say **why** she thinks women have them, and link it to slavery.
Frame: (1) claim, (2) reason (moral beings), (3) phrase one, (4) phrase two, (5) the link to abolition.
solution: Angelina Grimké argues that rights do not depend on sex: they belong to every human being because every human being is a moral being.
She writes that 'human beings have rights, because they are moral beings', so the same moral standard applies to men and women.
From that she concludes that 'whatever it is morally right for man to do, it is morally right for woman to do', including speaking in public against slavery.
She refuses to recognize separate men's rights and women's rights, only human rights.
The argument ties her two causes together: the same principle that condemns slavery condemns denying women a public voice.
exercises.why: Pulling out a thesis and its best evidence is what every job that reads documents asks of you.

exercises.title: Discussion: how the delegates use language to critique democracy
exercises.prompt: In 4 to 5 sentences, explain how the Declaration of Sentiments uses language to critique American democracy. Give two specific examples.
hints: Put the two declarations side by side: what did they copy, and what did they change?
The critique works because of the copying. Say why a reader in 1848 couldn't easily reject it.
Examples: 'all men and women are created equal'; 'man' in place of the King as the tyrant; the list of grievances; the demand for the vote.
solution: The Declaration of Sentiments critiques American democracy by copying the Declaration of Independence almost word for word.
It opens 'all men and women are created equal', showing that the nation's founding promise had left out half its people.
It replaces the King with 'man' as the tyrant, and lists grievances against men just as 1776 listed grievances against George III, such as forcing women to obey laws they had no voice in making.
By using the country's most respected language, the delegates made it hard to reject their demands, especially the vote, without rejecting the principles of 1776.
exercises.why: Using an opponent's own principles as your argument is one of the most effective moves in law, politics and negotiation.
